content: Papain is a hydrolase enzyme found in the papaya (Carica papaya) and mountain papaya (Vasconcellea cundinamarcensis). It is composed of 212 amino acids, stabilized by three disulfide bridges. Its three-dimensional structure features two distinct structural domains separated by a cleft, which houses the enzyme's active site. This active site contains a catalytic triad, similar to that of chymotrypsin, consisting of three amino acids: cysteine-25 (from which the enzyme derives its classification), histidine-159, and asparagine-158. The enzymatic mechanism of papain involves the cleavage of peptide bonds. This process begins with the deprotonation of cysteine-25 by histidine-159. Asparagine-158 plays a critical role in orienting the imidazole ring of histidine-159 to facilitate this deprotonation. Once deprotonated, cysteine-25 performs a nucleophilic attack on the carbonyl carbon of a peptide bond, releasing the amino-terminal portion of the peptide and forming a covalent acyl-enzyme intermediate. The enzyme is subsequently deacylated by a water molecule, releasing the carboxy-terminal portion of the peptide. In immunology, papain is known for its ability to cleave immunoglobulins (antibodies) into three fragments: two 50 kDa Fab fragments (antigen-binding regions) and one 50 kDa Fc fragment (crystallizable region). Papain has been used for centuries in South America for its ability to break down tough meat fibers. It is commercially available as a component in powdered meat tenderizers, commonly found in supermarkets. When made into a paste with water, papain is also used as a home remedy for treating jellyfish stings, bee stings, wasp stings, and possibly stingray wounds by breaking down the protein toxins in the venom. Additionally, it is the main ingredient in certain first-aid creams, such as Stop Itch and Stop Itch Plus, which are popular in Australia. In cell culture preparations, papain is used to dissociate cells. A 10-minute treatment of small tissue pieces (less than 1 mm³) with papain begins breaking down the extracellular matrix molecules that hold cells together. After this treatment, a protease inhibitor solution must be applied to halt the enzyme's activity, as prolonged exposure could lead to complete cell lysis. The tissue is then triturated (passed up and down through a Pasteur pipette) to create a single-cell suspension. Papain is also an ingredient in enzymatic debriding preparations, such as Accuzyme, which are used in the care of chronic wounds to remove dead tissue. It can be found in some toothpastes and mints as a teeth-whitening agent. However, its whitening effect is minimal due to its low concentration and rapid dilution by saliva, requiring several months of use to achieve noticeable results. Papain is typically produced as a crude, dried material by collecting latex from the fruit of the papaya tree. The latex is obtained by scoring the neck of the fruit, where it either dries on the fruit or drips into a container. This latex is then further dried and classified as a crude material. A purification step is necessary to remove contaminants, involving the solubilization and extraction of the active papain enzyme system through a government-registered process. The purified papain is supplied either as a powder or in liquid form.
